updates.title: 2027 UTME Bootcamp registration is open
updates.body: Our free UTME Bootcamp for the 2027 cohort has begun. Secure your spot, get a study plan across every JAMB subject, and start practising today.

updates.title: New student intake — limited pilot places
updates.body: We're admitting a small pilot group of students for tutoring and the Academy Hub. Early applicants get priority onboarding and mentorship.

updates.title: Purpose-Driven Scholar award
updates.body: Dedicated students who keep their study streaks and top the Weekly Scholar League can earn fee waivers and free premium access. Consistency is rewarded.

updates.title: AI Literacy program added to the curriculum
updates.body: Every G.O.C student now learns to use AI responsibly as a study partner — building independent thinking, not dependence. It's baked into the learning path.

updates.title: Live Zoom classes now paired with the app
updates.body: Attend interactive live classes on Zoom, then reinforce every lesson with practice and CBT mocks in the Academy Hub between sessions.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capital letters: The chairman’s remarks were TERSE.
questions.explanation: “Terse” means brief and abrupt — saying much in few words.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capital letters: The policy had a DETRIMENTAL effect on trade.
questions.explanation: “Detrimental” means harmful, so its opposite is “beneficial”.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Complete the sentence: If he ______ earlier, he would have caught the bus.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: “if + past perfect” pairs with “would have + past participle”.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Choose the word whose underlined vowel sound is different from the others.
questions.explanation: “Bread” has the short /e/ sound; the others use the long /iː/ sound.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Choose the correct option: Each of the students ______ a copy of the syllabus.
questions.explanation: “Each” is singular, so it takes the singular verb “has”.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: In the sentence “The meeting was called off”, the expression “called off” means the meeting was
questions.explanation: To “call off” something is to cancel it.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: The manager insisted that every worker ______ present at the briefing.
questions.explanation: After “insist that” the subjunctive is used, so the base form “be” is correct.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: In not more than 60 words, explain the difference between a formal and an informal letter, and give one situation in which each is appropriate.
questions.expected: A formal letter uses an impersonal, respectful tone, avoids contractions and slang, and carries both the writer’s and the recipient’s addresses with a formal salutation and closing — appropriate for official matters such as a job application. An informal letter is personal and conversational, allows contractions, and carries only the writer’s address — appropriate for writing to a friend or relative.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Write a topic sentence for a paragraph arguing that reading widely improves writing, then give two supporting points.
questions.expected: A suitable topic sentence states the claim clearly, e.g. “Wide reading is the surest way to become a better writer.” Supporting points may include: exposure to varied sentence patterns and vocabulary that the writer then reuses; and familiarity with how ideas are organised and paragraphs are linked, which improves the writer’s own structure. Award marks for a clear topic sentence (4) and two relevant, developed points (3 each).

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: Simplify $(2^3 \times 2^5) \div 2^4$.
questions.explanation: Add the indices when multiplying and subtract when dividing: $3 + 5 - 4 = 4$, so the answer is $2^4$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: If $3x - 7 = 11$, find $x$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: Find the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon.
questions.explanation: The sum of the interior angles is $(n - 2) \times 180^\circ$, so for a hexagon $(6 - 2) \times 180^\circ = 720^\circ$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: The mean of 4, 7, $x$ and 10 is 8. Find $x$.
questions.explanation: The total must be $4 \times 8 = 32$. Since $4 + 7 + 10 = 21$, $x = 32 - 21 = 11$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: Find the gradient of the straight line joining the points $(1, 2)$ and $(4, 11)$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: Evaluate $\log_{10} 8 + \log_{10} 125$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: The 3rd term of an arithmetic progression is 11 and the 7th term is 27. Find the common difference.
questions.explanation: Four steps separate the 3rd and 7th terms, so $4d = 27 - 11 = 16$ and $d = 4$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The SI unit of electric charge is the
questions.explanation: Charge is measured in coulombs; the ampere measures current, the volt potential difference and the ohm resistance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A body starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at $4\ \text{m/s}^2$ for 5 seconds. Find its final velocity.
questions.explanation: $v = u + at = 0 + (4 \times 5) = 20\ \text{m/s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation: Momentum has both magnitude and direction; the others are scalars.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Convert 27 °C to kelvin.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 4 m. Calculate its speed.
questions.explanation: $v = f\lambda = 50 \times 4 = 200\ \text{m/s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A transformer has 200 turns in the primary coil and 1,000 in the secondary. If the primary voltage is 40 V, the secondary voltage is
questions.explanation: $\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p} = 5$, so $V_s = 40 \times 5 = 200\ \text{V}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A machine with a velocity ratio of 5 has an efficiency of 80%. Find its mechanical advantage.
questions.explanation: Efficiency $= \frac{MA}{VR}$, so $MA = 0.8 \times 5 = 4$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: State Ohm’s law and explain one condition under which it does not hold.
questions.expected: Ohm’s law: the current flowing through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends, provided temperature and other physical conditions remain constant. It fails when the temperature of the conductor changes appreciably, and it does not apply to non-ohmic devices such as filament lamps, semiconductor diodes, gases and electrolytes. Award marks for a correct statement including the constant-conditions proviso (6) and one valid limitation (4).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A stone is thrown vertically upwards with a velocity of 20 m/s. Taking $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$, calculate the maximum height reached and the total time of flight.
questions.expected: At maximum height the final velocity is zero, so $h = \frac{u^2}{2g} = \frac{400}{20} = 20\ \text{m}$. Time to reach the top $= \frac{u}{g} = \frac{20}{10} = 2\ \text{s}$, and since the motion is symmetrical the total time of flight is 4 s. Award marks for the height with working (5) and the total time (5).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The general molecular formula of alkanes is
questions.explanation: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula $C_nH_{2n+2}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a physical change?
questions.explanation: Melting is reversible and forms no new substance, so it is a physical change.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: How many moles are present in 44 g of carbon(IV) oxide? [C = 12, O = 16]
questions.explanation: The molar mass of $CO_2$ is $12 + 32 = 44$ g/mol, so $n = \frac{44}{44} = 1$ mole.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: During electrolysis, oxidation takes place at the
questions.explanation: Anions migrate to the anode and lose electrons, so oxidation occurs there.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A solution with a pH of 3 is
questions.explanation: A pH below 7 is acidic; pH 3 indicates a fairly strong acid.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which gas turns lime water milky?
questions.explanation: Carbon(IV) oxide forms insoluble calcium trioxocarbonate(IV) with lime water, giving the milky appearance.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the oxidation number of manganese in $KMnO_4$?
questions.explanation: Potassium is $+1$ and each oxygen is $-2$, giving $1 + x - 8 = 0$, so $x = +7$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Define electrolysis and state two industrial applications of it.
questions.expected: Electrolysis is the decomposition of an electrolyte by the passage of an electric current through it in the molten or aqueous state. Industrial applications include: electroplating of metals; the extraction of reactive metals such as aluminium and sodium from their molten ores; the refining or purification of copper; and the manufacture of chlorine and sodium hydroxide from brine. Award marks for the definition (4) and two valid applications (3 each).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Explain, with an equation, why alkanes undergo substitution rather than addition reactions with chlorine.
questions.expected: Alkanes are saturated: every carbon atom is joined by single covalent bonds and already holds the maximum number of hydrogen atoms, so there is no double or triple bond for a reagent to add across. Chlorine therefore replaces a hydrogen atom instead. In the presence of sunlight: $CH_4 + Cl_2 \to CH_3Cl + HCl$. Award marks for the explanation based on saturation (6) and a correct balanced equation (4).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The basic structural and functional unit of life is the
questions.explanation: All living things are built from cells, which are the smallest units able to carry out life processes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which organelle is the site of photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which traps the light energy used in photosynthesis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart is the
questions.explanation: The pulmonary vein is the exception among veins: it carries oxygenated blood, from the lungs to the left atrium.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In humans, the sex chromosomes of a normal male are
questions.explanation: Males carry one X and one Y chromosome; females carry two X chromosomes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is an excretory organ in mammals?
questions.explanation: The kidneys remove urea, excess water and salts from the blood as urine.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Organisms that manufacture their own food from simple inorganic substances are called
questions.explanation: Producers, mainly green plants, are autotrophic and form the first trophic level.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A cross between two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt × Tt) gives a phenotypic ratio of
questions.explanation: The offspring are TT, Tt, Tt and tt — three tall to one short, a 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Define photosynthesis and write the balanced overall equation for the process.
questions.expected: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy trapped by chlorophyll to convert carbon dioxide and water into carbohydrate, releasing oxygen as a by-product. Overall equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, in the presence of light and chlorophyll. Award marks for a definition mentioning light energy, chlorophyll and the raw materials (6) and a correctly balanced equation (4).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: State three differences between arteries and veins.
questions.expected: Any three of the following: arteries carry blood away from the heart while veins carry blood towards it; arteries carry oxygenated blood (except the pulmonary artery) while veins carry deoxygenated blood (except the pulmonary vein); arteries have thick muscular elastic walls and a narrow lumen while veins have thin walls and a wide lumen; veins contain valves to prevent backflow while arteries do not; blood in arteries is under high pressure and flows in spurts, whereas blood in veins is under low pressure and flows smoothly. Award 3 marks per valid, clearly stated difference.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which technique is most suitable for separating a mixture of sand and water?
questions.explanation: Sand is insoluble in water, so filtration separates the insoluble solid from the liquid.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Common salt can be recovered from its aqueous solution by:
questions.explanation: Salt is soluble in water; evaporating off the water leaves the dissolved salt behind as crystals.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The most suitable method for separating a mixture of iodine and sodium chloride is:
questions.explanation: Iodine sublimes (passes directly from solid to gas) on gentle heating, leaving the non-subliming sodium chloride behind.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which of these mixtures can be separated using a separating funnel?
questions.explanation: Water and kerosene are immiscible liquids that settle into two layers; a separating funnel separates immiscible liquids.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Crude oil is separated into its various fractions in a refinery by:
questions.explanation: The components of crude oil have close, overlapping boiling points, so a fractionating column is needed to separate them.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A mixture of ethanol and water, which are miscible liquids with close boiling points, is best separated by:
questions.explanation: Fractional distillation, using a fractionating column, separates miscible liquids whose boiling points are close together.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which technique would best separate the coloured pigments present in a leaf extract?
questions.explanation: Chromatography separates the components of a mixture based on their differing solubility and movement on a stationary phase.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is used to separate a mixture of iron filings and sulphur powder?
questions.explanation: Iron filings are attracted by a magnet, leaving the non-magnetic sulphur powder behind.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The process of obtaining pure crystals of copper(II) sulphate from its impure aqueous solution is called:
questions.explanation: Crystallization is used to obtain pure solid crystals of a solute from a hot saturated solution as it cools slowly.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Decantation is most suitable for separating:
options: A solid from a liquid in which it has settled
Two immiscible liquids of similar density
A soluble solid from its solvent
questions.explanation: Decantation involves carefully pouring off the liquid from a settled solid (sediment) without disturbing it.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which apparatus is essential for fractional distillation but is not required for simple distillation?
questions.explanation: The fractionating column provides repeated vaporisation-condensation cycles that separate liquids with close boiling points.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Centrifugation is particularly useful for separating:
options: A suspension whose particles are too fine to filter easily
A solution into its solute and solvent
questions.explanation: Centrifugation spins a mixture at high speed, rapidly sedimenting fine suspended particles that would filter only slowly.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Winnowing is a traditional method used to separate:
options: Grains from chaff using a current of air
questions.explanation: Winnowing uses moving air (wind or a fan) to blow away the lighter chaff, leaving the heavier grains behind.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The statement that all matter is made up of tiny particles that are in continuous, random motion is known as the:
questions.explanation: The kinetic theory of matter states that particles of matter are in continuous, random motion, colliding with one another and their container.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The spreading of the smell of perfume throughout a room is best explained as an example of:
questions.explanation: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The random, erratic movement of smoke particles observed under a microscope, caused by bombardment from air molecules, is known as:
questions.explanation: Brownian motion is the erratic movement of visible particles caused by constant, random bombardment by smaller, invisible particles, and is evidence for the particulate nature of matter.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: In which state of matter are the particles most closely packed and possess the least kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: In a solid, particles are held in fixed positions close together and only vibrate about those positions, so they have the least kinetic energy of the three common states.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: An atom of chlorine has atomic number 17 and mass number 35. The number of neutrons present in the atom is:
questions.explanation: Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 35 − 17 = 18.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Naturally occurring chlorine consists of two isotopes: chlorine-35 (75%) and chlorine-37 (25%). The relative atomic mass of chlorine is:

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The relative atomic mass (RAM) of an element is defined as the average mass of one atom of the element compared with:
options: 1/12 the mass of one atom of carbon-12
The mass of one atom of hydrogen-1
1/16 the mass of one atom of oxygen-16
questions.explanation: By international agreement, relative atomic mass is measured on a scale where one atom of carbon-12 is assigned a mass of exactly 12, i.e. relative to 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Which of the following is a fundamental (base) physical quantity in the SI system?
questions.explanation: The SI base quantities are length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity; force, velocity and pressure are all derived from these.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The SI base unit of luminous intensity is the:
questions.explanation: Luminous intensity is one of the seven SI base quantities, and its base unit is the candela (cd); lumen and lux are derived units.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Which of the following derived quantities has the SI base units kg·m²·s⁻³?
questions.explanation: Power = energy/time = (kg·m²·s⁻²)/s = kg·m²·s⁻³. Force is kg·m·s⁻², energy is kg·m²·s⁻², and pressure is kg·m⁻¹·s⁻².

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In terms of mass (M), length (L) and time (T), the dimension of pressure is:
questions.explanation: Pressure = force/area = (MLT⁻²)/L² = ML⁻¹T⁻².

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A student records the length of a wire as 24.50 cm using an instrument that reads to the nearest 0.01 cm. The number of significant figures in this measurement is:
questions.explanation: In 24.50, the digits 2, 4, 5 and the trailing zero (which is significant because it follows a decimal point) all count, giving 4 significant figures.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The accepted value of the acceleration due to gravity is 9.8 m/s². A student's experiment gives a value of 9.6 m/s². The percentage error in the student's result, to one decimal place, is:

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Which instrument is most appropriate for accurately measuring the diameter of a thin wire of about 0.5 mm?
questions.explanation: The micrometer screw gauge has a much smaller least count (about 0.01 mm) than a vernier caliper or a metre rule, making it the most suitable for very small, precise lengths.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The least count (smallest reading obtainable) of an ordinary vernier caliper is usually:
questions.explanation: A standard vernier caliper has a least count of 0.01 cm (0.1 mm), obtained by dividing one main-scale division by the number of divisions on the vernier scale.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The least count of a standard micrometer screw gauge is:
questions.explanation: A standard micrometer screw gauge, with a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular scale, has a least count of 0.01 mm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A micrometer screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular (thimble) scale. Its least count is:
questions.explanation: Least count = pitch ÷ number of divisions on the circular scale = 0.5 mm ÷ 50 = 0.01 mm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: When using a micrometer screw gauge, the term 'zero error' refers to:
options: The error caused by worn threads on the spindle
The reading shown on the scale when the jaws are fully closed but do not read exactly zero
The difference between two independent measurements of the same object
The error caused by viewing the scale from an angle
questions.explanation: Zero error occurs when the micrometer does not read exactly zero with the jaws (or anvil and spindle) fully closed, and must be corrected for in every subsequent reading.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A micrometer screw gauge has a negative zero error of −0.02 mm. If the observed reading for an object is 5.46 mm, the corrected (true) reading is:
questions.explanation: True reading = observed reading − zero error = 5.46 mm − (−0.02 mm) = 5.48 mm; a negative zero error is subtracted, which adds to the observed reading.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: On a vernier caliper with a least count of 0.01 cm, the main scale reads 3.2 cm and the 4th vernier division coincides exactly with a main-scale line. The reading is:
questions.explanation: Reading = main scale reading + (coinciding vernier division × least count) = 3.2 cm + (4 × 0.01 cm) = 3.24 cm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Systematic errors in an experiment, such as a constant zero error, are best reduced by:
options: Taking a single, very careful reading
Properly calibrating the instrument against a known standard
Increasing only the number of trials, without checking the instrument
questions.explanation: Unlike random errors, systematic errors affect every reading in the same direction and by roughly the same amount, so they can only be removed by identifying and correcting the fault, usually through calibration.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Random errors that arise from unpredictable small variations in successive readings are best minimized by:
options: Using a more expensive instrument only
Taking several readings and calculating the average
Correcting for the instrument's zero error
Reading the scale from an oblique angle
questions.explanation: Random errors scatter about the true value in no fixed direction, so averaging several independent readings reduces their overall effect on the final result.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Parallax error in reading a scale occurs when:
options: The instrument has not been calibrated
The observer's eye is not placed directly perpendicular to the scale and pointer
The scale has too many divisions marked on it
Two different instruments give different readings for the same quantity
questions.explanation: Parallax error arises because the apparent position of a pointer against a scale changes with the viewing angle, so the eye must be positioned perpendicular to the scale to avoid it.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A car travels at a constant speed of 72 km/h. Expressed in metres per second, this speed is:

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The density of a certain substance is 2.5 g/cm³. Expressed in the SI base unit of kg/m³, this density is:
questions.explanation: Since 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³, a density of 2.5 g/cm³ converts to 2.5 × 1000 = 2500 kg/m³.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A length is recorded as 4600 m, which is ambiguous as to the number of significant figures intended. Written in standard (scientific) form to show exactly two significant figures, it should be expressed as:
questions.explanation: Scientific notation removes the ambiguity of trailing zeros; writing the value as 4.6 × 10³ m makes it clear that only two significant figures (4 and 6) are intended.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Which of the following pairs consists entirely of derived SI units?
questions.explanation: The newton (kg·m·s⁻²) and pascal (kg·m⁻¹·s⁻²) are both derived units, formed from combinations of base units; metre, kilogram, ampere, kelvin, second and candela are all SI base units.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The branch of biology concerned with the identification, naming and classification of living organisms is called:
questions.explanation: Taxonomy is the branch of biology dealing with the description, identification, naming and classification of organisms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The basic unit of classification of living organisms is the:
questions.explanation: The species is the smallest and most fundamental unit in taxonomic classification, consisting of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following represents the correct order of classification categories from the broadest to the most specific?
options: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom
Kingdom, Class, Phylum, Family, Order, Genus, Species
Phylum, Kingdom, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
questions.explanation: The standard taxonomic hierarchy runs from the broadest category, Kingdom, down through Phylum, Class, Order, Family and Genus, to the most specific, Species.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In binomial nomenclature, the scientific name given to an organism consists of:
questions.explanation: Binomial nomenclature gives every organism a two-part Latin name made up of its genus (capitalized) followed by its species (lowercase).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Man is placed in the genus Homo and the species sapiens. Written correctly according to the rules of binomial nomenclature, this is:
questions.explanation: In binomial nomenclature, the genus name is capitalized and the species name is written in lowercase, giving Homo sapiens.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is a key feature used to separate the kingdom Monera from the other four kingdoms?
options: Absence of a true, membrane-bound nucleus
Ability to move from place to place
questions.explanation: Organisms in kingdom Monera are prokaryotic, meaning they lack a true, membrane-bound nucleus, unlike organisms in the other four kingdoms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which cell structure, made up largely of microtubules, is responsible for pulling chromosomes apart during cell division?
questions.explanation: Spindle fibres, built from microtubules, attach to chromosomes at their centromeres and pull the sister chromatids apart during anaphase.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Microtubules are hollow, cylindrical structures built up from subunits of the protein:
questions.explanation: Microtubules are polymers of the globular protein tubulin, arranged as hollow tubes within the cytoskeleton.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a function of microtubules in a cell?
options: Forming the spindle apparatus during mitosis
Providing tracks along which organelles move within the cell
Helping to maintain and determine the shape of the cell
questions.explanation: Storing genetic information is the role of the nucleus (and its DNA), not of microtubules, whose roles include the mitotic spindle, intracellular transport tracks and cell shape.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Cilia and flagella, which enable movement in some cells, are built mainly from:
questions.explanation: Cilia and flagella have an internal core (axoneme) of microtubules arranged in a characteristic pattern, which produces their whip-like or beating movement.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following structures is present in a typical plant cell but absent from a typical animal cell?
questions.explanation: Plant cells possess a rigid cellulose cell wall surrounding the cell membrane, which is absent in animal cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is typically found in an animal cell but not in a plant cell?
questions.explanation: Centrioles, which organize microtubules during cell division, are found in animal cells but are absent from most plant cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The large, fluid-filled sac that helps maintain turgor and stores cell sap in a mature plant cell is the:
questions.explanation: The large, permanent central vacuole of a plant cell stores cell sap and, by taking up water, exerts pressure that keeps the cell turgid.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following organelles is common to BOTH plant and animal cells?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria, the site of aerobic respiration, are present in both plant and animal cells, unlike the cell wall, chloroplast and large permanent vacuole, which are typically plant-cell features.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The movement of water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential is called:
questions.explanation: Osmosis is the passive movement of water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane from a region of higher to a region of lower water potential.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The movement of substances against a concentration gradient, which requires the expenditure of metabolic (ATP) energy, is called:
questions.explanation: Active transport moves substances from a region of lower to a region of higher concentration, against the gradient, and therefore requires ATP energy.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: When a plant cell is placed in a concentrated (hypertonic) salt solution, water leaves the cell by osmosis and the cell membrane shrinks away from the cell wall. This condition is called:
questions.explanation: Plasmolysis is the shrinking of the cytoplasm and pulling away of the cell membrane from the cell wall, caused by excessive water loss in a hypertonic solution.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The organelle often described as the 'control centre' of the cell, because it contains the hereditary material (DNA), is the:
questions.explanation: The nucleus houses the cell's DNA and controls the cell's activities, including growth, metabolism and reproduction, earning it the name 'control centre'.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The small, dense body found within the nucleus that is responsible for the production of ribosomes is the:
questions.explanation: The nucleolus, a dense region within the nucleus, is where ribosomal RNA is synthesised and ribosome subunits are assembled.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The structure that separates the contents of the nucleus from the cytoplasm, and is perforated with pores that allow the exchange of materials, is the:
questions.explanation: The nuclear envelope is a double membrane, perforated with nuclear pores, that encloses the nucleus and controls the passage of materials between it and the cytoplasm.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: The chairman refused to ______ his statement even after being confronted with the facts.
questions.explanation: 'Retract' means to withdraw or take back a statement, which fits the context of refusing to withdraw what was said.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Despite the heavy rainfall, the trekkers were determined to ______ their journey to the summit.
questions.explanation: 'Proceed' means to continue or go on with an action, which is the meaning required in this context.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: The twins are so alike that it is difficult to ______ one from the other.
questions.explanation: 'Distinguish' means to recognise a difference between two similar things, fitting the sense of telling the twins apart.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: The manager's decision was final and ______; no appeal could change it.
questions.explanation: 'Irrevocable' means unable to be changed or reversed, which agrees with the idea that no appeal could alter the decision.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: He was so ______ by the loss of his job that he could not sleep for days.
questions.explanation: 'Distraught' means extremely upset or distressed, matching the described reaction of being unable to sleep after losing his job.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Neither the students nor the teacher ______ aware of the change in the examination schedule.
questions.explanation: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it — here, the singular 'the teacher' — so the singular verb 'was' is correct.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: 'All that glitters is not gold.' This statement means that:
options: Not everything that looks attractive is genuinely valuable
Gold is the only thing that glitters
questions.explanation: The proverb warns that attractive or impressive appearances do not always reflect true worth or value.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: 'A stitch in time saves nine.' This proverb best teaches that:
options: Sewing should always be done quickly
Prompt action prevents bigger problems later
Nine is considered a lucky number
Time cannot be saved once lost
questions.explanation: The proverb teaches that dealing with a small problem promptly prevents it from growing into a much larger one later.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Statement: 'Only members who have paid their dues may vote at the meeting.' From this statement, it can correctly be inferred that:
options: A member who has not paid dues cannot vote
Payment of dues is optional for voting
questions.explanation: Since only dues-paying members may vote, it follows directly that a member who has not paid dues is excluded from voting.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: 'It is better to be alone than in bad company.' This statement suggests that:
options: One should always live in isolation
Bad companionship is worse than solitude
Company of any kind is undesirable
Being alone is always preferable to being with others
questions.explanation: The statement compares two specific situations — solitude and bad company — and judges bad company to be the worse of the two, not company in general.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: All mammals are warm-blooded. All whales are mammals. It therefore logically follows that:
questions.explanation: Since every whale is a mammal, and every mammal is warm-blooded, it validly follows that every whale is warm-blooded.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Every student in the class passed the examination. Chidi is a student in the class. It follows that:
options: Chidi may or may not have passed
Chidi is not in the class
questions.explanation: Since every student in the class passed, and Chidi is a student in that class, it follows with certainty that Chidi passed.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: No reptiles have feathers. All birds have feathers. It logically follows that:
questions.explanation: Since birds all have feathers but no reptile has feathers, no bird can be a reptile.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: If it rains, the match will be postponed. It is raining. Therefore:
options: The match will continue as planned
It is not certain what will happen to the match
questions.explanation: Given the rule 'if it rains, the match will be postponed' and the fact that it is raining, it validly follows that the match will be postponed.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: All squares are rectangles. Figure X is not a rectangle. It follows that:
options: Figure X is not a square
Figure X may be a square
questions.explanation: Since every square is a rectangle, anything that is not a rectangle cannot be a square either; so Figure X is not a square.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: John is taller than Peter. Peter is taller than James. It therefore follows that:
options: John and James are of the same height
Peter is the tallest of the three
questions.explanation: By the transitive property of 'taller than', if John is taller than Peter and Peter is taller than James, then John must be taller than James.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: 'He who pays the piper dictates the tune.' This statement implies that:
options: Musicians should always be paid promptly
Whoever provides the funding controls how things are done
Tunes are more important than payment
questions.explanation: The saying means that the person who finances or funds an activity has the right and power to control how it is carried out.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Statement: 'The library will be closed to all students during the examination period, except those with special permission.' Based on this statement, a student without special permission during the examination period will:
options: Not be allowed into the library
Be allowed in only during the evening
questions.explanation: Since access during the examination period is restricted to students with special permission, a student without such permission will be denied entry.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: The committee members could not agree on a single candidate, so the decision was ______ to the following week.
questions.explanation: 'Deferred' means postponed to a later time, which fits the context of putting off the decision to the next week.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: The new government policy is aimed at reducing waste and promoting ______ use of resources.
questions.explanation: 'Prudent' means careful and sensible, which fits the idea of using resources wisely to reduce waste.

notes.subject: Use of English
notes.title: Subject–Verb Agreement
notes.body:
A verb must agree with its subject in number: a singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. The difficulty is finding the real subject, because words often sit between it and the verb.

In "the box of pencils is on the table", the subject is "box", not "pencils" — the phrase "of pencils" does not change the number.

Subjects joined by "and" are plural, but subjects joined by "or", "either...or" or "neither...nor" agree with the part nearest the verb. Words like everyone, each, nobody and somebody are singular, however plural they feel.

Exam tip: read past the words between the subject and the verb before you choose.

notes.subject: Use of English
notes.title: Reading for the Nearest Meaning
notes.body:
Lexis questions ask for the option nearest in meaning to a word as it is used in the sentence, not its dictionary meaning in general. The sentence is the evidence.

Work in three steps. First read the whole sentence and decide whether the word is positive, negative or neutral. Second, eliminate the options that carry the wrong feeling. Third, test the remaining options by substituting each one into the sentence.

Exam tip: an option that is a synonym in some other context is the commonest trap. Substitution catches it.

notes.subject: Mathematics
notes.title: Quadratic Equations
notes.body:
A quadratic equation has the form $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, where $a$ is not zero. You can solve it by factorising, by completing the square, or with the quadratic formula, which always works:

$$x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$$

The part under the root, $b^2 - 4ac$, is the discriminant. If it is positive there are two distinct real roots; if it is zero the roots are equal; if it is negative there are no real roots.

Exam tip: try factorising first. It is faster than the formula when the numbers are small, and most examination questions are built to factorise.

notes.subject: Mathematics
notes.title: The Laws of Indices
notes.body:
Indices are a shorthand for repeated multiplication, and every rule follows from that. Multiplying powers of the same base adds the indices, $a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}$; dividing subtracts them, $a^m \div a^n = a^{m-n}$; raising a power to a power multiplies them, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$.

Two special cases are worth memorising because they are tested constantly. Any non-zero number to the power zero is 1, so $a^0 = 1$. A negative index means a reciprocal, so $2^{-3} = \frac{1}{8}$. A fractional index is a root: $8^{\frac{1}{3}} = 2$.

Exam tip: write every number in the question to the same base before you start. Most index questions collapse in one line once you do.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Acceleration
notes.body:
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time. It is a vector, so it has both a size and a direction: an object slowing down is still accelerating, just in the direction opposite to its motion.

For uniform acceleration, $a = \frac{v - u}{t}$, where $u$ is the initial velocity, $v$ the final velocity and $t$ the time taken. The SI unit is the metre per second squared, $\text{m/s}^2$.

On a velocity-time graph, the acceleration is the gradient of the line and the area under the line is the distance travelled.

Exam tip: check the units before you calculate. A velocity given in km/h must be divided by 3.6 to become m/s.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Ohm’s Law
notes.body:
Ohm’s law states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature stays constant. In symbols, $V = IR$.

In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere and the resistances add, $R = R_1 + R_2$. In a parallel circuit the potential difference is the same across each branch, and the reciprocals of the resistances add: $\frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}$.

Exam tip: redraw the circuit before you calculate. Most mistakes in this topic are mistakes about which components are in series and which are in parallel, not about arithmetic.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Alkanes
notes.body:
Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons: they contain only carbon and hydrogen joined by single covalent bonds. Because every carbon carries as many hydrogen atoms as possible, they are described as saturated.

Their general formula is $C_nH_{2n+2}$, which lets you work out any member. When $n = 1$ you get methane, $CH_4$; when $n = 2$ you get ethane, $C_2H_6$; when $n = 3$, propane, $C_3H_8$.

Alkanes are generally unreactive, but they burn in air and undergo substitution reactions with halogens in the presence of sunlight.

Exam tip: memorise the first four names in order — methane, ethane, propane, butane.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Moles and the Avogadro Constant
notes.body:
A mole is an amount of substance containing as many particles as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12: $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ particles, the Avogadro constant.

Three relationships do most of the work. Number of moles equals mass divided by molar mass, $n = \frac{m}{M}$. Number of moles equals number of particles divided by the Avogadro constant, $n = \frac{N}{N_A}$. For a gas at s.t.p., number of moles equals volume divided by $22.4\ \text{dm}^3$.

Exam tip: write down which of the three you have been given before choosing a formula. Nearly every mole calculation is one of these three, or two of them joined by a balanced equation.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: The Cell as a Unit of Life
notes.body:
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all living things. Plant and animal cells share a nucleus, cytoplasm and a cell membrane, but a plant cell also has a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole.

The nucleus holds the chromosomes and controls the activities of the cell. The mitochondrion releases energy from food in respiration, which is why hard-working cells such as muscle and liver cells contain very many of them.

Exam tip: questions often turn on a single difference. Chloroplasts and a cellulose wall are plant only; centrioles are animal only.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Photosynthesis
notes.body:
Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light energy trapped by chlorophyll, releasing oxygen as a by-product.

It happens in two stages. The light stage splits water and stores energy; the dark stage uses that energy to fix carbon dioxide into sugar. The rate is limited by whichever factor is in shortest supply — light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration or temperature.

Exam tip: a graph in this topic is almost always about a limiting factor. Look for where the curve levels off and ask what has run short.

affirmations: I am a purpose-driven scholar. Today I study with focus.
Every question I attempt makes me sharper.
I don't chase luck — I build mastery, one topic at a time.
My effort today is my score tomorrow.
I can understand anything if I take it step by step.
Small steps, every single day, become big results.
I study to understand, not just to pass.
